messages.subject: ar1 sometimes fits what looks like an intercept-only model?
messages.subject_clean: ar1 sometimes fits what looks like an intercept-only model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am exploring some hierarchical time-series models using INLA. I have noticed something strange. Here is a basic example:

A simple ar1 model
mod = function(y) {
  require(INLA)
  z = 1:length(y)
  myData = list(y=y,z=z)
  formula = y ~ f(z,model="ar1",constr=T)
  m = inla(formula,data=myData,family="gaussian",
            control.predictor=list(link=1))
  return(m)
}

Some simple simulated data:
n = 100
theta = arima.sim(n=n,list(ar=0.75),sd=0.7) +10 ; plot(theta)
y = rnorm(n,mean=theta,sd=0.1)   ; lines(y,col="darkblue",lwd=2)
m = mod(y)
lines(m$summary.fitted.values[,1],col="green",lwd=2)

Sometimes this works as expected, with the rho parameter retrieved, and the fitted values are nearly identical to the original y data:

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-nzd_dcfhkpY/VIcqTwwRQqI/AAAAAAAAAPE/o5egrbHJqnM/s1600/Image.png>
Then other times, I generate another data set in the exact same manner (re-run this code), and the fitted values are essentially a straight-line, like an intercept-only model:

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-soUrCtjfFfk/VIcqW4Rq2CI/AAAAAAAAAPM/2vVseeG3Uzo/s1600/Image1.png>

When this happens, the rho parameter on the ar1 is always estimated to be negative, when it is supposed to be positive. My guess is I've done something weird in the simulation, but when I use arima() in R I can always retrieve the rho parameter without any problems on the exact same data that INLA has issues with. I've also tried very similar models in JAGS and never have this same problem. This problem only becomes weirder when I try to explore Poisson time-series counts. Any advice/ideas on what I'm doing wrong would be hugely appreciated!

Thanks so much,
Kathryn

Hi

what happens is that it goes to a different interpretation of the data,
and not the one you want. the main issue is the inital values, which for
some datasets makes it goes to the wrong place. the source for the
problem is the intercept, which is 10, in your case. which simply fools
the optimizer, and then it fail to turn.

simply setting a higher initial value for the data precision will fix
the problem, and runs fine for (at least) 1000 trials.

H

mod = function(y) {
  require(INLA)
  z = 1:length(y)
  myData = list(y=y,z=z)
  formula = y ~ f(z,model="ar1",constr=T)
  m = inla(formula,data=myData,family="gaussian",

      control.family = list(
          hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 10))),
          control.predictor=list(link=1))
}

for(i in 1:1000) {

n = 100
theta = arima.sim(n=n,list(ar=0.75),sd=0.7)

y = rnorm(n,mean=theta,sd=0.1)
m = mod(y)
err = mean(abs(y - m$summary.fitted.values[,"mean"]))
if (err > 0.01) print(c(i, err))
}

--
Håvard Rue

messages.subject: Binomial test
messages.subject_clean: Binomial test
messages.body_plain:
Hi to all,

I am trying to use INLA for identifying genes with allele-specific difference in a diploid hybrid. After processing the raw RNA-seq reads, what we get is simply the number of reads from paternal and maternal allele for each gene.

set.seed(12345)

data <- data.frame(paternal=as.integer(rnorm(10,100,20)),maternal=as.integer(rnorm(10,90,30)))

rownames(data) <- paste("gene", 1:10, sep="")

data

There are several packages designed to identify the differentially expressed genes between the two alleles. One of the simplest ways is using Binomial test for each gene (usually followed by multiple test correction, but not here).

apply(data, 1, function(x) binom.test(x)$p.value)

Cutoff at p<0.05 gives 3 genes with allelic difference.

Recently I found people prefer to use INLA to do this (Connelly et al, 2014, Plos Genetics), as follows:

   Let Rp, Rm represent the number of reads from paternal and maternal alleles, respectively.

   Rp| Rp+Rm, pp ~ Binomial(Rp+Rm , pp)

   Logit(pp) = log (pp/(1-pp)) + εi

     with εi ~ N(0, σ2) representing random effect.

Then posterior estimation of log(pp/(1-pp)) could be used to identify genes with allelic difference.

So I tried this method using the code:

library(INLA)

Ntrials <- apply(data, 1, sum)

episilon <- rnorm(10)

result <- inla(paternal ~ 1 + episilon, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=Ntrials)

I guess the intercept of the formula represents the posterior estimation. So my questions are:

1) Am I right so far?

2) How to get a posterior estimation for each gene/row?

3) How to integrate two replicates (two samples for each row)?

Thanks in advance

Best regards,

Jason

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

I think epsilon_j should be estimated and thus be included as a random effect. However, I am actually not sure what the exact model formulation of Connelly et al, 2014, Plos Genetics is and tried to derive it from their paper on page 9. It looks like that they have a separate intercept for each j, which seems a bit strange as the included an additional iid random effect epsilon_j as well.  The model would be

Ntrials <- apply(data, 1, sum)

data$idx <- 1:nrow(data)
data$idx2 <- 1:nrow(data)
formula <- paternal ~ factor(idx2) + f(idx, model="iid") -1
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=Ntrials)

and you could inspect the intercepts using summary(result) or result$summary.fixed. Alternatively, having only one intercept and the random effect epsilon_j the model should be

formula <- paternal ~ 1 + f(idx, model="iid")
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=Ntrials)

However, then you would need to look at the results for the linear predictor in order to get a result for "each row", i.e.

result$summary.linear.predictor

I am not sure, if you are aware of the work of Mark van de Wiel

http://biostatistics.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2012/09/16/biostatistics.kxs031.full

He wrote the R-package ShrinkBayes (http://www.r-inla.org/related-projects/shrinkbayes-by-mark-van-de-wiel) on top of INLA which can be used for RNA-seq data.

I hope that I could help you a bit.

Best regards,
Andrea

messages.subject: linear combination SPDE predictions
messages.subject_clean: linear combination SPDE predictions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I would like to calculate the sum of spatial predictions after projecting the SPDE random effects onto un-observed locations. Is there a way to approximate linear combination of these spatial predictions made by SPDE?

Please advise attached an example code. The population consists of 999 locations. Suppose 99 locations are sampled. I would like to estimate the total of the responses  from all 999 locations.

## simulated data
library(geoR)
n <- 999
dat <- grf(n,cov.pars=c(1,0.2))
ii <- sample(n,99) ## survey sample site
ldat <- data.frame(dat$coord[ii,],dat$data[ii])
colnames(ldat) <- c("ax","ay","y")

## define SPDE model
loc <- as.matrix(ldat[,c("ax","ay")])
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc,boundary=list(inla.nonconvex.hull(loc,0.1,0.15),inla.nonconvex.hull(loc,0.2,0.2)),max.edge=c(0.1,0.5))
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)
spatial.A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,loc)
stack <- inla.stack(data=list(y=ldat[,"y"]),A=list(spatial.A,1),effects=list(list(i=1:spde$n.spde),list(intercept=rep(1,nrow(ldat)))),tag="data")
f.geo <- y ~ -1 +intercept  + f(i,model=spde)

## make projection to population
Afull <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,loc=dat$coords)
stk.rf <- inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),A=list(Afull,1),effects=list(list(i=1:spde$n.spde),list(intercept=rep(1,nrow(Afull)))),tag="pred")
stack.full <- inla.stack(stack,stk.rf)

## fit model
geo.inla.full  <- inla(f.geo,family="gaussian",data=inla.stack.data(stack.full,spde=spde),control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.full),compute=T))

## extract marginals
ind <- inla.stack.index(stack.full,tag="pred")$data
pred <- round(geo.inla.full$summary.linear.pred[ind,], 4)

## how to calculate the posterior marginal for this?
sum(pred[,1])

Thanks
dong

messages.subject: Why does lambda increase with more data for a simple RW2 model?
messages.subject_clean: Why does lambda increase with more data for a simple RW2 model?
messages.body_plain:
I am applying RW2 to the Tokyo data, like the example in the INLA manual. I get a mode for lambda of 7550.
However, if I just double the data (repeat n and y once in the data set, with time going to 2x366 instead of 366), I get mode lambda of 10400.

I wouldn't expect mode lambda to change: shouldn't the marginalized likelihood for Tokyo2 just be the square of the marginalized likelihood for Tokyo? Shouldn't that result in the same mode?

I have also tried this with another method and lambda doesn't change -- so I assume that somehow, I am misinterpreting the INLA output.
I think the likelihood for realization y should be

lambda ^ (-1/2) * exp( - 0.5 * lambda * sum( (y[n+2] - 2y[n+1] + y[n])^2 ) * Prob(data | y)

and then you integrate over y.

What am I getting wrong here?

Code:

data(Tokyo)
formula <- y ~ f(time, model='rw2', cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001))-1
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", Ntrials=Tokyo$n, data=Tokyo,
control.inla=list(strategy='laplace'))

#Repeat Tokyo data (data set now twice as
#long with same information)
Tokyo2 = rbind(Tokyo, Tokyo)
Tokyo2$time = 1:nrow(Tokyo2)
result2 <- inla(formula, family="binomial", Ntrials=Tokyo$n, data=Tokyo2,
control.inla=list(strategy='laplace'))

Output:

> result$summary.hyperpar
                       mean       sd 0.025quant
Precision for time 13308.66 8953.281   3212.327
                   0.5quant 0.975quant     mode
Precision for time 11074.79    36648.6 7550.448

> result2$summary.hyperpar
                       mean       sd 0.025quant
Precision for time 15460.45 8465.951   5083.729
                   0.5quant 0.975quant    mode
Precision for time 13521.41   37181.73 10419.3

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Why does lambda increase with more data for a simple RW2 model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I _would _ expect the mode for lambda to change (even if one took all precautions to make sure the units were consistent when changing the model). Binomial data with small n (in this case 2) is very weakly informative for the parameters of the latent model, so I would expect the prior to dominate. Doubling the size of the model and data injects more information about the roughness, so the data starts to inform the lambda-posterior.
Also, note that the predictive intervals are very wide.

Finn L
